question: A logistics firm proposes a workflow in which Claude reads supplier refund disputes and sends the final decision straight to the supplier with no review. Which two features of the proposal make it inappropriate? Select two.
options: A) Refund thresholds are revised each quarter, so the standing instructions would have to be updated several times a year.
B) Nobody in the firm is answerable for any individual determination, because no person sees a case before it is sent.
C) Once the decision reaches the supplier it has already taken effect, so a wrong outcome cannot quietly be undone.
D) Disputes arrive as long email threads, and Claude works far less reliably with threads than it does with structured forms.
E) The firm receives too few disputes each month for an automated workflow to save any meaningful amount of staff time.
correct_answers: B) Nobody in the firm is answerable for any individual determination, because no person sees a case before it is sent.
C) Once the decision reaches the supplier it has already taken effect, so a wrong outcome cannot quietly be undone.
explanations: Keeping instructions current is ordinary maintenance and would apply to any well-run workflow, reviewed or not.
Correct. Accountability for each individual outcome is a separate problem from reversibility: no person is answerable for any single decision.
Correct. Sending a determination externally makes it effectively irreversible, and low reversibility is a strong signal that a human must be in the loop.
Reading and summarising email threads is well within normal capability, so the format is not what makes the proposal unsuitable.
Low volume might weaken the business case, but it is not a governance reason to reject the design.
